e: Quo Vadis (Henryk Sienkiewicz, 1896)

Sienkiewicz's novel is set in Nero's Rome. It begins around AD 63 and ends with Nero's fall. Its main thread is the love between the patrician Marcus Vinicius and the Christian Lygia; its background is the great fire of 64 and the persecution of the Christians.

This is a literary walk: it follows the plot of the novel, not a historical account. The places are named by the novel itself. Where it gives only a district, the stop is at a nearby point shown on the map, and the text says so. Chapter numbers in parentheses follow Jeremiah Curtin's English translation (1896); they may differ in other editions. The real fire has its own walk among the historical walks.
Aulus Plautius's house on the Vicus Patricius

At the start of the novel Petronius, Nero's “arbiter of elegance,” and his nephew Marcus Vinicius, just back from the eastern campaign, have themselves carried in a litter to the house of Aulus Plautius on the Vicus Patricius (chapter 2). Vinicius had earlier recovered here from a dislocated arm and fallen in love with Lygia, who was being raised in the house. Lygia is the daughter of a Lygian king who came to Rome as a hostage; Aulus and his wife, Pomponia Graecina, raise her as their own child.

Aulus Plautius and Pomponia Graecina are real people. Aulus led the conquest of Britain in AD 43. According to Tacitus, Pomponia was tried in AD 57 on a charge of “foreign superstition,” and her husband acquitted her before a family court (Annales 13.32). The novel turns this into her being a secret Christian.

The novel puts Petronius's house on the southern slope of the Palatine, “near the Carinae” (chapter 2). This is inaccurate: the Carinae lay northeast of the Palatine, between the Velia and the Oppian.
Lygia in the imperial palace

Vinicius asks Petronius to intercede so that he can have Lygia. On Nero's order a centurion takes the girl from Aulus's house to the Palatine, to Caesar's house, where Acte, Nero's former mistress, takes her into her care (chapters 5–7).

Lygia is also taken to the imperial feast (chapter 8). The drunken Vinicius presses himself on her; at the end of the feast Acte and Ursus carry her to Acte's rooms. There Lygia learns that Caesar has given her to Vinicius, and that she will be taken to his house that same evening (chapter 8).

In AD 63 Nero's palace on the Palatine was the Domus Tiberiana and the Domus Transitoria; the novel speaks only of “the Palatine” and “Caesar's house.” The stop is therefore the Domus Tiberiana, on the side of the hill facing the Forum.
Ambush in the Carinae

In the evening slaves carry Lygia in a litter to Vinicius's house, which stands in the Carinae. A feast is already being prepared there. As the procession turns toward the Carinae in the dark, armed men attack it; the slaves think it is Caesar and his companions out for fun, as Nero often was at night in the Subura (chapter 10).

The attackers are Lygia's supporters, among them Ursus, the girl's giant Lygian servant. Ursus takes Lygia in his arms and carries her off toward the Subura. When the bloodied slaves return, Vinicius in his rage kills Gulo, his old nurse, with a bronze lamp, and has the others flogged until morning (chapter 10).

That same night he sets out to search for her himself: he goes through the Esquiline, the Subura and the Vicus Sceleratus, around the Capitol, over the Fabrician bridge to the island, and from there into the district across the Tiber (chapter 11). The stop is the Clivus ad Carinas, the street leading into the district.
By night at the Viminal gate

Lygia is tracked down for Vinicius's money by Chilo Chilonides, a dubious Greek “philosopher.” He learns that the Christians gather at night in the Ostrianum, where a great apostle is to speak, and that Lygia will be there (chapters 17–19).

Vinicius sets out in disguise with Chilo and the wrestling champion Croton. The novel describes their route: through the Vicus Patricius, along the Viminal to the old Viminal gate, near the plain where Diocletian's baths were later built, then on past the remains of the Servian wall (chapter 20).

The location of the gate on the map is conjectural; this stretch of the Servian wall is shown on one of the map's layers.
The Nomentan Gate and the Ostrianum

They leave the city through the Nomentan Gate; according to the novel they have to hurry to get out before it is closed (chapter 19). In the novel the Ostrianum is an old underground cemetery between the Via Salaria and the Via Nomentana, enclosed by a wall overgrown with ivy; it lies beyond the edge of the map.

All the Christians of Rome gather in the cemetery to hear the Apostle Peter. Vinicius watches the ceremony from a dark corner and catches sight of Lygia. The novel describes Peter's sermon at length, and how his listeners almost see the Sea of Galilee before them (chapter 20).

Christian tradition does indeed associate a cemetery called the Ostrianum with the work of the Apostle Peter.
Across the Tiber

At dawn Vinicius and his companions follow Lygia and her escort into the district across the Tiber, where the girl lives in a narrow street. When Vinicius tries to force his way in, Ursus kills Croton in the gateway and badly injures Vinicius (chapter 21). Chilo flees.

The Christians nurse the wounded Vinicius in the house; Lygia is with him, and the Apostle Peter visits him too. Here Vinicius begins to change: the Christians forgive him, and this shakes him deeply (chapters 22–25).

The novel does not give the exact location of the house, only that it is across the Tiber, in a narrow street. Later Lygia lives in the house of Linus, on the Vicus Judaeorum (chapter 43). The stop is the Cestian bridge, which links the island with Trastevere and also appears in the novel.
The outbreak of the fire

Vinicius is with Nero's court at Antium when the news arrives: Rome is burning. According to the novel the fire broke out at the Circus Maximus, in the part facing the Palatine and the Caelian, and with incredible speed engulfed the center of the city (chapter 42). This agrees with Tacitus's account (Annales 15.38).

Nero returns as well. He climbs onto the arches of an aqueduct, which the novel calls the “Appian aqueduct,” and with a golden lute, surrounded by his entourage, sings of the fall of Troy above the burning city (chapter 46). Below, the people murmur; Petronius rides out on horseback in front of the crowd and promises them bread and games.

Here the novel works up one of the ancient rumors about the fire, which Tacitus mentions only as hearsay. The Aqua Appia ran mostly underground; it has no row of arches on the map.
Vinicius's ride to Rome

Vinicius leaps onto a horse at once and gallops toward Rome on the Via Appia, changing horses everywhere along the way without stopping (chapter 42). As he nears the city the crowd grows ever larger: refugees, carts, people camping among the tombs and gardens. The doors of the temple of Mars, which according to the novel stood near the “Porta Appia,” have been broken down by the crowd so that they can spend the night inside (chapter 43).

With great difficulty Vinicius reaches the gate, but he cannot get into the city toward the Porta Capena: the crowd and the heat make it impossible. So he takes some soldiers with him, turns back, skirts the city to the south across the Via Latina and the Ardea and Ostia roads, crosses the Tiber at a village called Vicus Alexandri, and sets off along the Via Portuensis toward the district across the Tiber (chapter 43).

The novel speaks of the Via Appia's city gate. In AD 64 the city gate here was the Porta Capena of the Servian wall; the Porta Appia of the Aurelian wall was built only two centuries later.
Along the Via Portuensis into the flames

The Via Portuensis leads straight into the district across the Tiber (chapter 43). At the gate he learns that most of the district has not yet been reached by the fire; only the alleys toward the island are burning. Linus's house on the Vicus Judaeorum stands right there; Vinicius finds it empty. On the way back the flames and smoke chase him toward the Via Portuensis, and he collapses.

He is picked up by Christians who are pulling down houses so that the fire will not reach the Via Portuensis. Among them he finds Chilo, who tells him that Linus went out two days earlier through the Nomentan Gate to the Ostrianum (chapter 43). Vinicius finds Lygia there and also speaks with the Apostle Peter (chapters 45–47).

Here too the novel closely follows the real fire: according to Tacitus, of the fourteen regions of the city three burned down completely, seven were badly damaged, and only four remained intact (Annales 15.40).
The Mamertine prison

The people want a scapegoat. Tigellinus, the commander of the guard, and Poppaea pin the arson on the Christians; Chilo betrays them. Lygia is arrested at her house and taken to the Mamertine prison (chapters 49–50). Vinicius and Petronius arrive at dawn, but the prison is already surrounded by guardsmen.

According to the novel's footnote, Lygia was not thrown into the Tullianum, the lowest, entirely underground part of the prison, where Jugurtha had once starved to death. A fever epidemic breaks out in the prisons; Lygia falls ill too (chapter 54).

This is the map's real Carcer: its lower chamber is the Tullianum, which Sallust also describes. According to the novel the Apostle Peter is later held here too, and his two guards, Processus and Martinianus, are baptized here (chapter 70).
The Esquiline prison and the arena

At night Lygia is moved to the Esquiline, to an improvised prison set up in the cellars of houses torn down to stop the fire; the novel describes it as better guarded than the Tullianum (chapters 56, 59). Vinicius gets in to see her disguised as a corpse-bearer, and they say farewell to each other. Tigellinus's house also stands on the Esquiline (chapter 53).

Meanwhile the Christians are being killed at the games. According to the novel, after the fire Nero had new amphitheaters built, mostly of wood, among them an enormous one (chapter 55). At the last evening games a German aurochs is driven in with Lygia tied to its horns; Ursus breaks the beast's neck with his bare hands. The people demand mercy, and Nero is forced to grant it (chapter 65).

The novel does not say where the amphitheater stood; the Colosseum was built only later, by the Flavians. Nor does it give the exact location of the Esquiline prison; the stop is the old Esquiline gate, which the novel also mentions.
Nero's gardens on the Vatican

Nero stages an evening spectacle in his Vatican gardens: Christians are tied to pitch-smeared posts and set alight as living torches (chapter 61). The crowd streams into the gardens over the Aemilian bridge and along the Triumphal Way, around Nero's circus.

Chilo rides in a chariot beside Nero. On one of the burning posts he recognizes Glaucus, the physician whom he himself betrayed. The sight breaks him: he cries out to the crowd that innocent people are dying here, and, pointing at Nero, names the emperor as the incendiary (chapter 61). His story is one of the turning points of the novel.

Here the novel follows Tacitus's account of the execution of the Christians in Nero's gardens (Annales 15.44). On the central line of the circus stood the obelisk that is now in the middle of St. Peter's Square.
Quo vadis, Domine?

The faithful persuade the Apostle Peter to leave the city. At dawn he sets out with the young Nazarius along the Via Appia toward Campania (chapter 69). On the way he stops, and in a vision Christ comes toward him. Peter asks: “Quo vadis, Domine?”, that is, “Where are you going, Lord?” The answer: if Peter abandons his people, he will go to Rome to be crucified again. Peter turns around and goes back to the city.

This scene gives the novel its title. The story comes from a late 2nd-century apocryphal text, the Acts of Peter; it is not among the historical sources.

At the traditional site there now stands the church of Domine Quo Vadis, about 800 meters south of the Porta Appia, beyond the edge of the map. The Porta Appia was built only in the 3rd century; at the time of the novel the Via Appia here still ran outside the city.
Peter's last journey

Peter is arrested and held in the Mamertine prison. Nero is not in Rome; according to the novel two of his freedmen, Helius and Polythetes, pass sentence. He is flogged, and the next day he is led out of the city toward the Vatican Hill (chapter 70). A huge crowd gathers in front of the gates; the faithful go with him. The soldiers lead him across the Pons Triumphalis, toward the Naumachia and the circus.

The novel remarks that the bridge of triumphs seemed, as if unwittingly, to proclaim the apostle's triumph.

The Pons Triumphalis is usually identified with the Neronian bridge, whose pier remains can be seen near today's Ponte Vittorio Emanuele when the water is low.
The deaths of Peter and Paul

Peter is crucified between the circus and the Vatican Hill (chapter 70). According to the novel, from the cross he looks at the city in the light of the setting sun and blesses it: “Urbi et orbi.” That same evening soldiers lead the Apostle Paul along the Ostian Way, through the Trigemina gate, to a place called Aquae Salviae, and behead him there.

The novel follows Christian tradition; contemporary sources say little about the year and circumstances of Peter's and Paul's deaths in Rome. Tradition places Peter's grave here, in the Vatican cemetery; the remains of the 2nd-century memorial have been found beneath St. Peter's Basilica.

At the end of the novel Petronius takes his own life at Cumae before Nero's death sentence can reach him (chapter 73). Vinicius and Lygia live in Sicily (chapter 72). The epilogue tells of Nero's fall and death.

Walks from novels

Literary walks: each follows on the map the plot of a novel set in Rome. They are not historical sources; the places are named by the novel itself, and the text points out where the novel departs from reality.
